Some updated photos of the S. minor var. okefenokeensis Charlton Co, GA plants. They're very big right now, but not gigantic. I chopped all of the plants down to the ground (deadheaded them) during the winter dormancy, and I have to do that because this population is planted too close to each other. I think if you space them out and keep the previous year's growth on until you have a few monster spring traps, they'll probably get bigger.

Even so, let's see: these may still produce giant fall traps! There's a ton of new growth pushing out right now. Photo taken 7/14/18:

posts.body_html:
Found an unusually green clone in this population! well, there's two clones like this: they're greener than all the rest, but what's really impressive is how yellow they can get! It reminds me of AF sarracenia in general: under optimal conditions, the green turns to neon yellow! Some of you might actually have this clone already, so if you got a minor giant from me from this population keep a close eye on it. I have divided this neon yellow- green clone in the past, and it has been mixed up with all the other divisions. Photos taken 2/10/19:




Different clone, but same concept. Notice the deep green face that contrasts with the yellower body:


For perspective, a normal colored clone from this population, although this is a dormant pitcher. they tend to color up during the fall and dormancy period:

posts.body_html:
It's really hard to tell from the pics, but many of these traps got absolutely gigantic this year! Initially, I thought these traps get big during the fall if it's really warm, but after seeing gigantic traps form during the fall after having very cool weather all summer long, I'm now convinced the way to get gigantic fall traps is to make sure the spring traps feed heavily! This past spring, every single trap in these trays were filled to maximum capacity with insects.

Pics taken late-ish August and early September 2021:

posts.body_html:
Thanks for asking Jgreen1025! I think the easiest way to describe it is, all else equal, the more room the roots have to grow, the bigger the plants can get! Of course, there's way more factors to it than that: you can't expect all your plants to get gigantic just by giving them an enormous amount of soil to grow in, they need the right genetics and environmental conditions to do that.

I use 100% peat, but you could hypothetically use many other carnivorous plant soil mixes and get the same results, provided the right environmental conditions are met.

posts.body_html:
Sept 14, 2021 22:10:26 GMT -5 meizzwang said:
.....the more room the roots have to grow, the bigger the plants can get ......provided the right environmental conditions are met.


I second this 100% having used this principle for 25 years. In my own collection all plants will get as large as they can when the roots are given room to run in adequate soil volume. If it is a single growth point, give it room. If it's a large genet, give it room. Especially the upright ones which naturally have more extensive root systems. More roots = more rhizome growth point development and larger leaves. The main roots from the rhizome will be thick and white with a vigorous downstream network. The individual plant will let you know with sulky size when it hasn't got enough room. Watch it boost away when it has.

Seedlings are perfect example also. Keep them moving year to year into more space to develop roots. Mature flowering plants will be the result in short order.

Combine this with lots of insects as Mike says for a winning situation. Insect volume is not a problem for outside grown collections and, in the feeding sense, a real advantage compared with glass houses.

Gorgeous minors Mike.

posts.body_html:
I've got one S. minor var. okefenokeensis from Charlton Co., GA and I think it's an absolutely lovely plant!


March 2019 - starting its first year with some nice overwintered pitchers.


June 2019 - For a small rhizome, I was pleasantly surprised to get such robust growth in year 1.


September 2019 - super skinny!


May 2020 - Yellow! 2020 was not a great year for this one, I originally potted it in some crappy long fibered sphagnum, and it spent all of 2019 growing on the patio of my college apartment being watered with some absolutely garbage-quality water. I should have repotted it!


June 2021 - Finally repotted. It started 2021 very late!


September 2021 - Filled in pretty well. Now you may be thinking, dang Clue, get that green okefenokeensis some sun, you shouldn't shade it to get that height!


But this is actually full sun! Here's the var. minor that grows about a foot away from it. The skinny, green pitchers really do a good etiolation impression.


Yellow!


November 2021 - Picked up some dormancy colors. These dark colors probably aren't too typical (I think this is quite a yellow clone), but the fresh peat and cool temperatures seem to help bring out the reds like most Sarracenia.


March 2022 - One of the few nice overwintered pitchers, also pretty yellow.


May 2021 - I was thinking that this plant was doing okay (at least better than 2020) but that it could be better. I don't move around my pots at all except to take them out for pictures; this is the angle I see the pot from every day, which is apparently the most unflattering angle, because

these views leave an impression!!



I think if I'd seen a var. okefenokeensis vs. var. minor photo like this, I would have got on the okefenokeensis train a lot earlier!

posts.body_html:
There were 94 or so mother plants jam-packed into 2 cement mixing tubs, and it's been that way for a very long time! This past winter, the plants were separated, divided, and given significantly more space to size up.

So far, they're doing very well this season, all things considered! My minor giants usually take a full season to recover after transplanting, but these seem to be growing full force! They might even get big this fall, we'll see! Pics taken 6/24/22:






One of the reasons they're doing so well is probably because they're feasting heavily right now! We had late rains which kept the native grasses green longer than normal, which in turn kept the insect populations much heavier for longer:
